newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to pull all troops out of Congo.
newsitem.headline: France to pull all troops out of Congo.

text.p: France will start pulling its troops out of Brazzaville on Sunday after completing the evacuation of French nationals from the strife-torn Congolese capital, the French Foreign Ministry said on Friday.

It said "Operation Pelican" to protect or fly out foreign nationals caught in fighting between the forces of President Pascal Lissouba and former Marxist president Denis Sassou Nguesso would end at 1600 GMT on Sunday.

"By this time, all French nationals who so wished will have been evacuated," it said. "As soon as Operation Pelican ends, the French military contingent will begin its disengagement with a view to a total pullout."

Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said all troops would leave the former French colony -- the 400 troops who were there before fighting started and the 850 reinforcements who were flown in with six light tanks to assist the evacuation.
"There will not be any French troops left in the Congo," he said. It was not clear how long the withdrawal would take.

French marines and foreign legionnaires, operating out of Brazzaville airport and making forays into the city, have flown out 4,300 foreign civilians, 1,550 of them French, to Libreville in Gabon since June 7.
France also has military bases in the region in Gabon, the Central African Republic and Chad.
The withdrawal announcement put paid to Sassou Nguesso's hopes that French troops could take part in an international force he has sought to enforce a ceasefire.
"For the ceasefire to be maintained, an international force must be deployed," he told the French daily newspaper Le Figaro.
But France has said its forces will not intervene in the nine-day-old conflict and would act solely to protect foreigners.
Sassou Nguesso said a scheduled presidential election on July 27 "could not take place without international control because Lissouba's people...are no longer qualified to organise the election."

Lissouba, also interviewed by Le Figaro, said there could be international observers, but it was up to the government to organise the election. He said he was neither for nor against a peace force but feared it would delay the poll.

Gunfire rang out sporadically on Friday but the city was calmer than previously. The conflict erupted on June 5 after government soldiers surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home as part of a crackdown on private militias and illegal possession of arms before the election.
Mediators led by Brazzaville mayor Bernard Kolelas said Lissouba and Sassou Nguesso would meet in Gabon on Sunday. But a spokesman for Lissouba could not confirm that he would attend.
